item.content:encoded:
The Gender and Diversity Lab (GDLab), an initiative of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Group, has launched a new Call for Research Proposals on “Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy.”

The call seeks research proposals that can generate rigorous, credible, and policy-relevant evidence on one of the most important questions facing economies in Latin America and the Caribbean: how government regulations, financial systems, fiscal policies, and labor-market reforms affect the economic opportunities available to women and men, and how public policy can help reduce gender differences in economic outcomes.

Through this initiative, GDLab and the IDB’s Institutions for Development Sector are looking to support research that goes beyond describing gender gaps. Instead, the call emphasizes causal research capable of determining whether particular policies, reforms, regulations, or interventions actually produce different outcomes for women and men.

Researchers are encouraged to develop studies that can provide practical evidence for governments, private-sector organizations, and multilateral institutions seeking to design more effective policies and programs.

The deadline for applications is September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon).

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity Details
Organizer GDLab, an IDB Group initiative, in collaboration with the IDB’s Institutions for Development Sector
Opportunity Call for Research Proposals
Research theme Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy
Geographic focus Latin America and the Caribbean
Eligible research countries One or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries
Research approach Rigorous quantitative causal research
Accepted methodologies Experimental, quasi-experimental, and structural models
Qualitative research Considered only when supporting the quantitative analysis
Funding Available under the funding categories specified in the official brochure
Application platform Oxford Abstracts
Deadline September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon)
Research outputs External peer review; potential consideration for the IDB Working Paper Series; academic publication encouraged

About the Research Call

Gender differences in economic opportunities can emerge from many aspects of economic and institutional systems. Regulations can influence whether women and men can enter particular occupations, establish businesses, access financial services, participate in the labor market, or benefit equally from economic reforms.

Similarly, fiscal policy can affect households, workers, businesses, and entrepreneurs differently depending on gender, income, employment status, family responsibilities, and access to economic resources.

The new GDLab call is designed to support research that investigates these relationships systematically.

Rather than simply asking whether a gender gap exists, researchers are expected to examine questions such as:

  • What causes differences in economic opportunities between women and men?
  • Which regulations create or reduce barriers to women’s economic participation?
  • Do financial policies affect women and men differently?
  • How do fiscal reforms influence women’s and men’s labor-market outcomes?
  • What happens when governments introduce a particular policy or regulatory reform?
  • Which interventions are effective at reducing gender disparities?
  • Are some policies more effective for certain groups of women or men?
  • What policy instruments can governments use to expand economic opportunities?
  • How can governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations use evidence to design more effective interventions?

The emphasis on causal research is particularly important because the organizers are seeking evidence that can help distinguish correlation from actual policy effects.

Main Objective of the Call

The central objective is to support rigorous causal research addressing two broad areas.

1. Understanding how reforms affect women and men differently

The call seeks research examining how regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms affect economic opportunities for women and men.

This could include studying whether a particular reform changes:

  • Labor-force participation
  • Employment
  • Earnings
  • Entrepreneurship
  • Business creation
  • Access to finance
  • Business growth
  • Occupational opportunities
  • Formal employment
  • Access to economic resources
  • Productivity
  • Economic mobility
  • Other relevant measures of economic opportunity

Researchers should be able to establish credible relationships between the policy or reform being studied and the resulting outcomes.

2. Identifying policies that can reduce gender differences

The second major objective is to understand how policy instruments can improve economic opportunities and reduce differences between women and men.

This moves the research from diagnosis toward solutions.

The strongest studies may therefore demonstrate not only that a gender gap exists, but also identify which policy interventions can effectively address the gap and under what circumstances.

What Topics Will the Research Call Prioritize?

The call focuses broadly on the relationship between economic opportunity, gender, regulation, fiscal policy, financial systems, and labor-market policies.

Researchers may investigate how different forms of government intervention influence women and men differently.

Potential research areas can include the following.

1. Regulatory Reforms

Regulations can have significant effects on people’s ability to participate in economic activity.

Research could examine how changes in regulations affect women and men in areas such as:

  • Employment
  • Entrepreneurship
  • Business registration
  • Business ownership
  • Occupational access
  • Labor-market participation
  • Business operations
  • Access to markets
  • Formalization
  • Economic activity

A strong proposal could investigate whether a regulatory reform removes barriers to women’s participation or unintentionally creates new constraints.

2. Financial Policies and Access to Finance

Access to financial services is another important component of economic opportunity.

Researchers could examine whether women and men experience different outcomes from:

  • Credit policies
  • Financial inclusion programs
  • Lending reforms
  • Access to business finance
  • Financial regulations
  • Credit guarantees
  • Digital financial services
  • Other financial policy instruments

The research could investigate whether financial reforms improve women’s ability to start, operate, or expand businesses and whether the effects differ from those experienced by men.

3. Fiscal Policy

Fiscal policies can influence economic decisions and opportunities through taxation, government spending, transfers, subsidies, and other mechanisms.

Researchers could examine whether fiscal reforms have different effects on women and men.

Possible questions could include:

  • Does a particular tax reform affect women and men differently?
  • Do government transfers increase women’s economic participation?
  • Can fiscal incentives encourage women’s entrepreneurship?
  • Do public spending programs improve women’s access to economic opportunities?
  • How do fiscal policies interact with household responsibilities?
  • Are certain fiscal instruments more effective at reducing gender disparities?

The objective would be to produce evidence that can inform future fiscal-policy decisions.

4. Labor-Market Reforms

Labor-market policies are directly connected to economic opportunity.

Researchers could study the effects of reforms involving:

  • Employment regulations
  • Labor-market participation
  • Working conditions
  • Employment protections
  • Formal employment
  • Wages
  • Hiring
  • Occupational mobility
  • Other labor-market outcomes

The research should examine whether particular policies create different effects for women and men and whether reforms can reduce existing disparities.

Why Causal Research Is Central to This Opportunity

One of the most important requirements of this call is that proposals use rigorous quantitative methods capable of establishing causal relationships.

This means that applicants should not simply present descriptive statistics showing that women and men have different economic outcomes.

For example, a study showing that women earn less than men would demonstrate a gender difference, but by itself it would not establish what caused that difference.

The call is interested in research that can answer stronger questions such as:

What was the effect of a specific policy, regulation, or reform on women’s economic outcomes compared with what would have happened without that intervention?

This distinction makes the methodological component of the proposal extremely important.

Methodologies That May Be Used

The call specifically identifies several rigorous quantitative approaches.

Experimental Designs

Experimental research can be used when researchers can credibly introduce or evaluate an intervention and compare outcomes between relevant groups.

For example, researchers could evaluate whether a particular policy intervention changes economic outcomes for women compared with an appropriate comparison group.

Quasi-Experimental Designs

Quasi-experimental methods can be particularly useful when researchers cannot randomly assign policies or interventions.

Depending on the research question and available data, appropriate approaches could include methods designed to exploit:

  • Policy changes
  • Regulatory reforms
  • Eligibility thresholds
  • Geographic variation
  • Timing differences
  • Other institutional or policy changes

The key requirement is that the chosen methodology must provide a credible strategy for identifying causal effects.

Structural Models

The call also allows the use of structural models.

These approaches can be useful when researchers want to model economic behavior and simulate how alternative policies or reforms could affect outcomes.

A structural approach may therefore allow researchers to examine not only the effect of an existing policy but potentially the implications of alternative policy scenarios.

Role of Qualitative Research

The call does not completely exclude qualitative research.

However, qualitative components will be considered only to the extent that they support the implementation of the quantitative analysis.

This means that a proposal centered primarily on qualitative interviews, focus groups, narratives, or descriptive case studies may not align well with the call’s methodological expectations.

A stronger approach would be to use qualitative information strategically to:

  • Inform the design of the quantitative research
  • Help understand the institutional context
  • Support interpretation of quantitative findings
  • Improve implementation of the research strategy
  • Help explain mechanisms behind quantitative results

The quantitative causal component should remain central.

Geographic Scope: Latin America and the Caribbean

A critical eligibility condition is the geographic focus of the research.

Only proposals analyzing one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries will be considered.

This means researchers should ensure that their proposed study has a clear connection to an eligible IDB borrowing member country.

Applicants should therefore verify the IDB’s official list of borrowing member countries before developing their proposal.

The geographic requirement is important because the call is designed to generate evidence directly relevant to economic and policy challenges in the Latin America and Caribbean region.

What Makes a Strong Proposal?

Although the final proposal should follow the detailed requirements in the official brochure, the description of the call provides several clear indications of what the organizers are seeking.

A competitive proposal should ideally demonstrate:

1. A clear research question

The proposal should clearly explain what economic or policy question it intends to answer.

2. A strong gender dimension

The research should meaningfully examine differences between women and men rather than simply mentioning gender as a secondary variable.

3. A clearly defined policy or reform

The study should identify the relevant regulation, financial policy, fiscal reform, labor reform, or other policy instrument being evaluated.

4. A credible causal identification strategy

The proposal needs to explain how the researchers will establish a causal relationship.

5. Appropriate quantitative data

Applicants should demonstrate that the necessary data are available or realistically obtainable.

6. Policy relevance

The research should have potential implications for real-world decision-making.

7. Actionable recommendations

The call particularly encourages proposals that can generate recommendations for:

  • Governments
  • Private-sector organizations
  • Multilateral organizations

This makes policy applicability an important feature of a potentially competitive proposal.

Potential Research Questions Applicants Could Explore

The following examples illustrate the type of questions that could fit within the broad theme of the call. They are illustrative research directions, not an official list of required topics.

Regulation

  • How does a change in business registration regulation affect women’s business creation?
  • Do regulatory reforms affect female-owned businesses differently from male-owned businesses?
  • Which regulatory barriers have the greatest effect on women’s participation in formal economic activity?

Finance

  • Does improved access to formal credit increase women’s entrepreneurship?
  • Do financial reforms produce different business outcomes for women-owned and men-owned enterprises?
  • What types of financial interventions most effectively reduce gender gaps in access to capital?

Fiscal Policy

  • How do changes in taxation affect women’s labor-force participation?
  • Do government transfers have different employment effects for women and men?
  • Can targeted fiscal policies increase women’s participation in economic activity?

Labor Markets

  • How do labor regulations influence women’s formal employment?
  • Do changes in employment protections affect women and men differently?
  • Which labor-market reforms are most effective at reducing gender disparities?

Again, the strongest proposal would need to translate such a question into a rigorous causal research design.

Why This Research Matters

Gender differences in economic opportunity are not simply individual-level issues. They can affect households, businesses, labor markets, productivity, income distribution, and broader economic development.

When women face barriers to employment, entrepreneurship, finance, or economic participation, economies may fail to use a significant portion of their available human capital.

Understanding which policies actually improve economic opportunities can therefore help governments allocate resources more effectively.

This is particularly important because policies that appear gender-neutral on paper can sometimes have different effects on women and men.

For example, a policy may technically apply equally to both groups but interact differently with:

  • Household responsibilities
  • Existing employment patterns
  • Access to financial resources
  • Business ownership
  • Occupational segregation
  • Labor-market participation
  • Access to formal institutions

Rigorous causal research can help policymakers identify these differences and design more effective interventions.

Policy Impact Is a Major Component

The call explicitly encourages research capable of generating actionable recommendations.

This means the ultimate value of a successful study should extend beyond academic publication.

Research findings could potentially help policymakers understand:

  • Which policies work
  • Which policies do not work
  • For whom policies work
  • How large the effects are
  • Whether effects differ by gender
  • What unintended consequences may exist
  • How policies could be improved
  • Whether an intervention can be scaled
  • How limited public resources could be allocated more effectively

The findings may also be relevant to private-sector organizations and multilateral institutions.

Potential Benefits for Selected Researchers

Selected studies will undergo external peer review, which can provide an additional layer of academic and methodological scrutiny.

Selected research may also be considered for publication in the IDB Working Paper Series.

In addition, the call encourages publication in academic journals.

For researchers, this means the opportunity can potentially provide more than research funding. A successfully completed project could also contribute to:

  • Academic research
  • Policy evidence
  • Regional economic policy discussions
  • Gender-equality research
  • Government decision-making
  • Institutional research outputs
  • Peer-reviewed publications

Funding Available

The call provides funding under categories specified by the organizers.

Because the exact funding amounts and corresponding requirements are detailed in the official brochure, applicants should review the brochure carefully before preparing their budgets and submitting their proposals.

Researchers should pay particular attention to:

  • Available funding categories
  • Maximum funding amounts
  • Eligible expenses
  • Research team requirements
  • Proposal requirements
  • Methodological expectations
  • Application documentation
  • Submission procedures

Applicants should not rely solely on summaries of the call when preparing a submission. The official brochure should be treated as the authoritative source for the complete funding and eligibility conditions.

Click HERE to learn more.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted online through the Oxford Abstracts platform.

The application process should be approached carefully because the proposal needs to demonstrate both substantive relevance and methodological rigor.

Step 1: Review the Official Call

Begin by reading the official brochure carefully.

Pay particular attention to:

  • Eligibility
  • Research priorities
  • Funding categories
  • Proposal requirements
  • Evaluation criteria
  • Submission requirements
  • Key dates

Step 2: Select an Eligible Country

Make sure the research analyzes one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries.

Step 3: Define the Research Question

Develop a precise question related to economic opportunities for women and men and the role of:

  • Regulation
  • Financial policy
  • Fiscal policy
  • Labor-market reform
  • Other relevant policy instruments

Step 4: Develop the Causal Strategy

Explain exactly how the research will establish causal effects.

The proposal should identify the appropriate quantitative methodology and demonstrate why it is suitable for the research question.

Step 5: Demonstrate Data Feasibility

Applicants should consider whether the necessary data exist and whether they can realistically be accessed and analyzed within the project’s scope.

Step 6: Explain Policy Relevance

Clearly explain how the findings could inform policy decisions.

Step 7: Develop Actionable Recommendations

Where possible, demonstrate how the research could translate evidence into recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations.

Step 8: Submit Through Oxford Abstracts

The completed application must be submitted through the designated Oxford Abstracts application platform before the deadline.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon).

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their proposals. Researchers should allow sufficient time to:

  • Review eligibility requirements
  • Develop the research question
  • Finalize the methodology
  • Verify data availability
  • Prepare the research team information
  • Develop the budget
  • Review supporting documentation
  • Complete the online application
  • Resolve any technical issues with submission

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The GDLab Call for Research Proposals on Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy offers an important opportunity for researchers studying gender differences in economic participation and the effectiveness of public policy in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The call is particularly suited to research teams capable of conducting rigorous quantitative causal analysis rather than purely descriptive or qualitative studies. Its emphasis on regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms creates a broad research space for investigators examining how policy decisions shape economic opportunities for women and men.

A particularly strong application is likely to combine a well-defined policy question, a credible causal identification strategy, appropriate quantitative data, a clear gender dimension, and strong policy relevance. Researchers are also encouraged to ensure that their findings can translate into actionable recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral institutions.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for up to five PhD scholarships at Monash University in Australia for researchers interested in examining the human, social, ethical, political, cultural, economic and creative consequences of artificial intelligence.

The Monash Arts “Shaping AI’s Future” PhD Scholarships are aimed particularly at researchers from the humanities, arts and social sciences who want to investigate how artificial intelligence is changing society and how people, institutions, cultures and political systems are simultaneously shaping the development and use of AI.

Rather than concentrating primarily on the engineering or technical development of artificial intelligence, these PhD opportunities focus on the human dimensions of AI.

Possible research areas include:

  • AI governance and public policy
  • Democracy and artificial intelligence
  • Digital inequality
  • Algorithmic discrimination
  • Human-AI relationships
  • Youth wellbeing and AI companionship
  • AI and ageing
  • Digital labour
  • Automation and employment
  • AI and creative industries
  • Music and generative AI
  • Screen aesthetics
  • Misinformation and communication
  • Public trust
  • Cultural representation
  • Ethics
  • Surveillance
  • Social cohesion
  • Machine agency
  • AI and knowledge production
  • Artificial intelligence in education
  • National security
  • Geopolitics
  • Environmental implications of AI

Up to five scholarships will be awarded through the Faculty of Arts at Monash University.

The scholarships provide a Research Living Allowance valued at AUD 41,100 per year at the 2027 full-time rate, paid as a tax-free stipend and indexed in accordance with applicable scholarship conditions. Additional allowances are available according to the relevant Research Training Program stipend scholarship rules.

The opportunity is open to appropriately qualified domestic and international applicants. The announcement also states that successful international candidates will receive tuition support in addition to the stipend.

Successful candidates will undertake their PhDs full-time and on campus at either the Clayton or Caulfield campus in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.

Applications close on:

Wednesday, 30 September 2026 at 11:55 PM AEST.

Successful candidates are expected to commence their PhD no later than 12 March 2027.

About the Monash University “Shaping AI’s Future” PhD Scholarships

Artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, is developing and spreading through society at extraordinary speed.

While much public discussion focuses on the technical capabilities of AI systems, Monash Arts argues that understanding artificial intelligence requires much more than engineering or computer science.

AI also raises fundamental questions about:

  • Human behaviour
  • Social relationships
  • Knowledge
  • Politics
  • Culture
  • Communication
  • Identity
  • Ethics
  • Employment
  • Inequality
  • Governance
  • Security
  • Creativity
  • Public institutions

The Faculty of Arts is therefore seeking doctoral researchers capable of investigating these broader dimensions of technological transformation.

The programme emphasizes research from the Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences, commonly abbreviated as HASS.

These disciplines provide theoretical, methodological and critical tools that can help explain how AI affects individuals and societies and how policy responses can be designed in ways that are effective, equitable and inclusive.

Why Monash Arts Is Funding Research on the Human Side of AI

AI is influencing increasingly large areas of everyday and institutional life.

Among the issues identified by Monash Arts are questions surrounding AI’s influence on:

  • Social cohesion
  • Knowledge production
  • Education
  • Culture
  • Geopolitical competition
  • National security
  • Institutional trust
  • Digital humanities
  • Personal and intimate relationships
  • Environmental sustainability
  • Ethics
  • Governance

These developments create an urgent need for research capable of informing future decision-making.

Monash Arts emphasizes that Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences researchers should play an active role in determining how AI is incorporated into society.

The challenge is not simply to ask:

“What can AI do?”

Researchers also need to ask questions such as:

  • How should AI be governed?
  • Who benefits from AI?
  • Who may be disadvantaged?
  • How does AI change relationships between people and institutions?
  • How might AI reinforce existing inequalities?
  • What happens to work when automation expands?
  • How does AI influence public trust and democracy?
  • How should culture, creativity and authorship change in an AI-driven environment?
  • How do people resist or reject AI?
  • How should society think about responsibility and machine agency?

These are precisely the kinds of questions the scholarship programme is designed to support.

Number of PhD Scholarships Available

Monash Arts is offering:

Up to five PhD scholarships

Selection will be competitive.

The scholarships are intended for applicants capable of undertaking advanced interdisciplinary research addressing current or emerging challenges created by artificial intelligence and wider digital transformation.

Applicants are not expected simply to replicate existing projects.

The programme seeks researchers who can demonstrate:

  • Intellectual curiosity
  • Research potential
  • Social awareness
  • Strong academic preparation
  • Understanding of the proposed field
  • Ability to develop a credible doctoral project

Scholarship Value

Successful candidates will receive a:

Research Living Allowance of AUD 41,100 per annum

This is the stated:

2027 full-time rate

The stipend is described as:

Tax-free

and is:

Indexed

Additional allowances may apply according to Monash University’s Research Training Program stipend scholarship conditions.

Applicants should consult Monash University’s current graduate research scholarship regulations for detailed rules governing payments, indexing and allowances.

Tuition Support for International Candidates

The programme announcement states that successful international candidates may receive:

  • Full stipend
  • Tuition support

This makes the scholarships especially relevant to international applicants who would otherwise face substantial international doctoral tuition costs in Australia.

Applicants should nevertheless review the formal scholarship conditions and final offer carefully because the specific tuition arrangements and scholarship components may depend on Monash graduate research rules.

Scholarship Duration

The opportunity is listed as a:

3.5-year fixed-term appointment

This provides sufficient time for candidates to complete a structured doctoral research programme.

The PhD must be undertaken:

  • Full-time
  • On campus

It is therefore not advertised as an online or distance PhD.

Where Will Successful Candidates Study?

Successful applicants will be based at either:

  • Monash University Clayton campus, or
  • Monash University Caulfield campus

Both campuses are located in the Melbourne metropolitan area in the state of Victoria, Australia.

The exact campus will likely depend on the research project, academic unit and supervisory arrangements.

About Monash University

Monash University is a large internationally connected Australian university with multiple campuses and global partnerships.

Successful PhD researchers will join a university environment with links across:

  • Australia
  • Asia
  • Europe
  • International research networks

Monash Arts describes itself as a diverse faculty supporting:

  • Disciplinary research
  • Multidisciplinary research
  • Interdisciplinary research

Research within the Faculty operates at multiple levels, including:

  • Individual experience
  • Communities
  • Societies
  • Regions
  • Nations
  • International systems

This broad intellectual environment is particularly relevant to AI research because artificial intelligence increasingly affects multiple areas of social life simultaneously.

International Mobility Opportunities

Successful candidates will have access to:

International mobility grants

These may provide opportunities to strengthen research through international collaboration or academic mobility.

Applicants should consult Monash University for the detailed eligibility and funding arrangements associated with specific mobility schemes.

Professional Development Opportunities

PhD scholars will also have access to:

Professional development training

This may support the transition from doctoral research into academic, policy, industry or research careers.

The programme is therefore intended not only to support thesis completion but also to strengthen participants’ broader research profiles.

Industry Engagement

Successful candidates may also access:

Opportunities for industry engagement

This feature is particularly relevant because AI governance and implementation increasingly involve collaboration between:

  • Universities
  • Technology companies
  • Governments
  • Regulators
  • Civil society
  • Creative industries
  • Policy organizations

Researchers interested in the practical impact of their work may therefore have opportunities to engage beyond academia.

Interdisciplinary Supervision

The scholarship call emphasizes:

Interdisciplinary supervision

AI-related societal questions rarely fit entirely within one academic discipline.

For example, an investigation of algorithmic discrimination could potentially involve:

  • Political science
  • Sociology
  • Law
  • Policy studies
  • Ethics
  • Data governance

Similarly, AI and creative labour might involve:

  • Cultural studies
  • Media studies
  • Labour studies
  • Sociology
  • Music
  • Creative practice

Interdisciplinary supervision can therefore help doctoral candidates address these complex questions from multiple perspectives.

Suggested Research Projects

Monash Arts has identified several possible research topics associated with academics already working in these fields.

Applicants are encouraged, where feasible, to align their proposals with these suggested projects.

However, candidates should discuss their proposed research with the relevant prospective supervisor before submitting an application.

1. Co-designing AI Companionship to Promote Young People’s Social Health and Wellbeing

Proposed supervisor: Dr Claire Tanner

This project focuses on:

AI companionship and young people’s social health and wellbeing.

The emergence of conversational AI and increasingly personalized AI systems raises important questions about how young people may interact emotionally or socially with technology.

The project creates space for research into how AI companionship might be designed, understood or evaluated in relation to youth wellbeing.

2. Public Resistance to and Rejection of AI in Everyday Life

Proposed supervisor: Professor Neil Selwyn

Much discussion of technological innovation assumes that people will inevitably adopt new technologies.

This project instead focuses on:

Resistance to AI

and:

Rejection of AI in everyday life.

It offers an opportunity to investigate why individuals or communities may choose not to adopt particular technologies and what those decisions reveal about:

  • Trust
  • Power
  • Autonomy
  • Social expectations
  • Technology adoption

3. AI for Inclusive CALD Ageing and Care Communication

Proposed supervisor: Dr Hui Huang

This project considers AI in the context of ageing and communication involving culturally and linguistically diverse communities, often described using the abbreviation CALD.

The research could contribute to questions surrounding:

  • Inclusive communication
  • Ageing
  • Care
  • Language
  • Cultural diversity
  • AI-mediated services

4. AI and the Future of Democratic Life: Participation, Persuasion and Public Trust

Proposed supervisor: Dr Charles Crabtree

This project addresses the relationship between:

  • Artificial intelligence
  • Democracy
  • Political participation
  • Persuasion
  • Public trust

AI increasingly influences how political information is produced, distributed and consumed.

Research in this area may therefore have important implications for democratic institutions and governance.

5. From Generative AI to Generative Futures in Music

Proposed supervisors: Dr Rod Davies and Dr Nicole Canham

The full proposed theme is:

From generative AI to generative futures in music: mapping future professionalism for evolving music labour markets.

This research focuses on the impact of generative technologies on:

  • Music
  • Professional identities
  • Creative labour
  • Employment
  • Future music industries

It may appeal particularly to researchers working across creative practice, cultural policy, music studies and labour research.

6. Human Craft, AI and the Future of Screen Aesthetics

Proposed supervisor: Dr Elliott Logan

This project focuses on how artificial intelligence may affect:

  • Human creative craft
  • Screen production
  • Visual aesthetics
  • Creative processes

The research offers an opportunity to investigate changing relationships between human creative practice and AI-supported or AI-generated media.

7. Human Labour and Automation in the Warehouse and Logistics Industry

Proposed supervisor: Dr Christopher O’Neill

This project addresses the relationship between:

  • Human labour
  • Automation
  • Warehousing
  • Logistics

AI and automation are transforming workplaces, particularly sectors characterized by data-driven monitoring and increasingly automated processes.

The project could contribute to wider discussions surrounding the future of work.

8. Auditing Algorithms: Detecting and Reducing Discrimination in AI-Driven Decisions

Proposed supervisor: Dr Charles Crabtree

Algorithmic systems increasingly influence decisions affecting individuals and communities.

This project focuses specifically on:

  • Algorithm auditing
  • Discrimination
  • AI-driven decision-making

The research has potentially significant implications for:

  • Equality
  • Governance
  • Regulation
  • Public policy
  • Institutional accountability

9. The Changing Nature of Digital Inequalities in an Age of AI

Proposed supervisor: Professor Neil Selwyn

Digital inequality has traditionally concerned differences in:

  • Technology access
  • Connectivity
  • Digital skills
  • Digital participation

AI introduces additional dimensions to these inequalities.

This project investigates how digital disadvantage may change in an increasingly AI-dependent society.

Can Applicants Propose Other AI Research Topics?

The call provides suggested topics but describes applicants as researchers interested in addressing the contemporary and future challenges associated with artificial intelligence and digital transformation.

Applications are expected to:

  1. Fit within the overall scope of the AI-focused scholarship call.
  2. Align, where feasible, with one of the proposed topics.
  3. Demonstrate an understanding of the proposed research area.

Applicants should therefore discuss any alternative idea with a prospective Monash supervisor before assuming that it fits the scholarship.

Who Should Apply?

Monash Arts welcomes applicants from diverse backgrounds across:

  • Humanities
  • Social sciences
  • Creative arts

Candidates should be interested in social, cultural, political or environmental challenges associated with the rapid development of AI.

Potential disciplinary backgrounds may therefore include:

  • Sociology
  • Political science
  • International relations
  • Public policy
  • Philosophy
  • Ethics
  • Media studies
  • Communication
  • Cultural studies
  • Anthropology
  • Law
  • Digital humanities
  • Creative arts
  • Music
  • Labour studies
  • Education
  • Related HASS disciplines

The exact academic background should align with the proposed PhD topic.

Academic Requirements

The selection committee will prioritize applicants holding an:

Australian Honours degree or equivalent international qualification

or:

Master’s degree

in a cognate discipline aligned with the proposed research project.

The qualification should demonstrate:

A significant research component.

Candidates should therefore have previous experience undertaking substantial independent research.

First-Class Honours / H1 Requirement

Preference will be given to candidates who have achieved:

First-Class Honours / H1 or equivalent

This is an important indication of the competitiveness of the scholarships.

International applicants whose universities use different grading systems should review Monash University’s equivalency rules.

Applicants should not simply convert their grades themselves and assume equivalence.

The Faculty of Arts graduate research admissions process determines whether international qualifications meet the relevant standard.

Significant Research Component

Candidates should have completed a substantial research component as part of their previous qualification.

Examples could include:

  • Honours thesis
  • Master’s dissertation
  • Research thesis
  • Substantial independent research project

Applicants should make this research preparation clear in their CV and application documents.

Applicants Who Already Have a PhD

Candidates who already hold a doctoral degree:

Will not be considered.

The scholarship is intended for applicants seeking their first PhD.

English Language Requirements

Candidates must meet the English-language proficiency requirements for PhD admission to the Monash Faculty of Arts.

Applicants who are required to submit an English test must include the relevant results with their application.

The exact requirements depend on Monash University’s graduate research admissions policies.

Prospective applicants should review:

https://arts.monash.edu/graduate-research/application-process/

before submitting their scholarship application.

Full-Time Enrollment Is Mandatory

Scholarship recipients must be enrolled:

Full-time

Part-time enrollment is not offered under the conditions stated in this call.

On-Campus Attendance Is Mandatory

Successful candidates must also study:

On campus

This means scholars should be prepared to live in or around Melbourne and undertake their research from the relevant Monash campus.

International candidates should therefore consider:

  • Australian student visa requirements
  • Relocation costs
  • Housing
  • Living costs
  • Health insurance
  • Travel arrangements

when preparing for potential study in Australia.

Research Proposal Discussion Is Required Before Applying

One of the most important application requirements is that candidates must:

Discuss their research proposal with an aligned prospective supervisor before submitting the application.

Applicants should therefore not submit directly without first identifying an appropriate supervisor.

This requirement allows candidates to determine whether:

  • Their topic fits the scholarship
  • Appropriate expertise is available
  • Their proposed project is feasible
  • The supervisor is interested in supporting the research

How to Approach a Prospective Supervisor

Applicants should ideally contact a potential supervisor with a concise and focused message.

A useful first approach may contain:

  • Your name
  • Current university or professional role
  • Academic background
  • Degree results
  • Research interests
  • Short description of your proposed PhD topic
  • Why the supervisor’s research is relevant
  • Mention of the “PhD Scholarships: Shaping AI’s Future” call
  • CV
  • Brief preliminary proposal where appropriate

Avoid sending a generic message to multiple academics without demonstrating familiarity with their research.

Application Documents

Applications must contain several supporting documents.

1. Cover Letter

Applicants must provide a:

Cover letter including a brief statement of suitability.

The letter should explain why the applicant is a strong candidate for the scholarship.

A strong letter could highlight:

  • Academic preparation
  • Previous research
  • Interest in AI and society
  • Relevant methodological experience
  • Fit with the proposed project
  • Fit with the supervisor
  • Career objectives

2. Draft Research Proposal

Candidates must submit a:

Draft research proposal

The proposal must:

  1. Fit within the scope of the “Shaping AI’s Future” scholarship call.
  2. Align, where feasible, with one of the proposed research areas.
  3. Demonstrate an understanding of the relevant discipline or research field.

This is likely to be one of the most important documents in the selection process.

What Should the Research Proposal Demonstrate?

A competitive proposal should make clear:

  • What problem the research addresses
  • Why that problem matters
  • What existing research already tells us
  • What remains unknown
  • What research question will be investigated
  • Which theoretical or conceptual framework may be useful
  • What methodology could be used
  • Why Monash is an appropriate environment
  • How the project relates to AI’s social, cultural, ethical or political dimensions

Applicants should follow the official Monash research proposal guidance rather than relying solely on generic PhD proposal formats.

3. Detailed Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a detailed CV.

The CV should include relevant information concerning:

  • Academic qualifications
  • Research projects
  • Research methods
  • Publications
  • Conference presentations
  • Professional experience
  • Relevant employment
  • Awards
  • Scholarships
  • Academic service

Applicants who have published work should provide a clear publication list.

4. Academic Records

Candidates must provide:

A full statement of academic records

This allows Monash to assess the candidate’s academic performance.

5. Degree Certificates

Applicants should provide relevant:

Degree certificates

Scanned copies of required certified documents must be uploaded.

6. Official Grading System

Applicants should include information concerning their institution’s:

Official grading system

where available.

This is particularly important for international candidates because Monash needs to determine Australian equivalency.

7. English-Language Results

Candidates should submit:

English-language proficiency test results

if these are required under Monash admission policies.

8. Two Academic Referees

Applicants must provide:

Names and contact details of two academic referees.

Ideally, referees should know the candidate’s research ability well.

Potential referees may include:

  • Master’s supervisor
  • Honours supervisor
  • Research project supervisor
  • Academic mentor
  • Lecturer familiar with the candidate’s research

All Supporting Documents Must Be in PDF Format

Applicants should upload supporting documents through the application system in:

PDF format

Candidates should check documents carefully before submitting.

How to Apply

Applications shall comprise:

  • A cover letter that includes a brief statement of the applicant’s suitability
  • A draft Research Proposal that (i) fits within the scope of this call for research, (ii) aligns, where feasible, with one of the proposed topics, and (iii) demonstrates some understanding of the area of research (e.g., discipline or field of study).
  • A detailed curriculum vitae, including a list of any published works, conference presentations and relevant work experience
  • A full statement of academic records, degree certificates and official grading system (if available), supported by scanned copies of relevant certified documentation
  • English language proficiency test results (if applicable)
  • Names and contact details of 2 academic referees

Once you have discussed your proposal with the prospective project supervisor, please submit your application via My.App and upload all supporting documentation in pdf format:

  • Select Admission Only as the Application Type
  • Select ‘Yes’ to indicate that you are applying for a scholarship for this research and enter “PhD Scholarships: Shaping AI’s Future” as the scholarship name under Research Program Funding of the application.
  • Select the relevant project supervisor as the name of the proposed main supervisor (final supervision arrangements to be confirmed upon appointment).

 Applications Close: Wednesday 30 September 2026, 11:55 pm AEST

Expected Starting Date

Successful applicants are expected to commence their PhDs:

No later than 12 March 2027

Candidates should therefore be prepared to:

  • Complete admissions requirements
  • Arrange relocation
  • Obtain an Australian visa where required
  • Arrange housing
  • Meet enrollment requirements

before the commencement deadline.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

1. Contact the Supervisor Early

This is not optional.

The call states that applicants are required to discuss the proposal with an aligned prospective supervisor before submission.

Begin this process well before September 30.

2. Do Not Treat It as a Computer Science Scholarship

The programme is explicitly focused on the:

Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences dimensions of AI.

Your proposal should therefore explain how AI relates to human or societal questions rather than merely proposing the development of a new machine-learning model.

3. Identify the Human Problem Behind the Technology

Strong proposals should begin with an important research problem.

Potential questions might concern:

  • Democracy
  • Inequality
  • Labour
  • Culture
  • Trust
  • Wellbeing
  • Ethics
  • Discrimination
  • Governance
  • Human relationships

Technology should be connected to a broader substantive question.

4. Demonstrate Interdisciplinary Thinking

AI affects multiple aspects of society simultaneously.

Applicants who can thoughtfully combine perspectives across relevant disciplines may be particularly well suited to the programme.

However, interdisciplinary does not mean unfocused.

Your research question still needs a clear intellectual foundation.

5. Show Strong Research Preparation

The scholarships are competitive.

Highlight evidence that you are prepared for doctoral research, such as:

  • Strong thesis performance
  • Publications
  • Conference presentations
  • Research assistant experience
  • Relevant methods training
  • Independent research projects

6. Explain Why the Research Matters

The scholarship emphasizes research capable of responding to contemporary and future challenges.

Explain how your project could contribute to:

  • Academic knowledge
  • Public policy
  • Industry practice
  • Regulation
  • Society
  • Public debate

depending on your topic.

7. Connect Your Proposal to the Supervisor

Do not simply list an academic as your proposed supervisor.

Explain why their expertise is relevant.

A credible intellectual connection will strengthen the application.

Key Details at a Glance

University: Monash University

Faculty: Monash Arts

Programme: PhD Scholarships: Shaping AI’s Future

Job number: 697891

Number available: Up to five

Location: Melbourne, Victoria, Australia

Campus: Clayton or Caulfield

Study mode: Full-time

Attendance: On campus

Duration: 3.5 years

2027 stipend: AUD 41,100 per year

Tax status: Tax-free stipend

Indexation: Yes

International tuition: Tuition support indicated for successful international candidates

Primary field: Human, social, cultural, political and ethical dimensions of AI

Previous PhD holders: Not eligible

Supervisor contact before application: Required

Expected commencement: No later than 12 March 2027

Deadline: 30 September 2026 at 11:55 PM AEST

Conclusion

The Monash University Shaping AI’s Future PhD Scholarships 2027 provide an outstanding opportunity for researchers who want to investigate artificial intelligence not simply as a technological innovation, but as a profound social, cultural, ethical and political transformation.

Monash Arts is offering up to five PhD scholarships, with successful candidates receiving a tax-free Research Living Allowance of AUD 41,100 per year at the 2027 full-time rate, together with applicable allowances. The programme announcement also indicates tuition support for successful international candidates.

The scholarships are intended for applicants from the humanities, arts, social sciences and related fields with strong research preparation and an interest in understanding the consequences of artificial intelligence for society.

Potential research areas include AI and democracy, public trust, digital inequality, algorithmic discrimination, automation and labour, youth wellbeing, ageing, creative industries, music, cultural production, communication and other aspects of AI’s rapidly evolving relationship with human life.

Successful candidates will undertake their PhDs full-time and on campus at Monash University’s Clayton or Caulfield campus in Melbourne and will have access to interdisciplinary supervision, professional development, international mobility opportunities, relevant AI research networks and opportunities for industry engagement.

Applicants should normally hold an Honours or Master’s qualification with a significant research component in a cognate field, with the selection committee prioritizing candidates demonstrating First-Class Honours/H1 or equivalent academic performance.

Candidates who already hold a PhD will not be considered.

Most importantly, applicants must discuss their research proposal with an appropriate prospective supervisor before submitting an application.

Applications require a cover letter, draft research proposal, detailed CV, academic records, degree certificates, grading information, English-language results where applicable and contact details for two academic referees.

The application deadline is:

30 September 2026 at 11:55 PM AEST

Successful scholars must be able to commence no later than: 12 March 2027

item.content:encoded:
The Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is now accepting applications from established academics and researchers interested in bringing their scholarly expertise into conversations about technology policy, digital rights, democracy, privacy, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, free expression, and the future of the internet.

Based in Washington, D.C., with remote participation allowed, the program creates a bridge between academic research and real-world public-interest technology policy. Rather than separating academic scholarship from policy development, CDT’s Non-Resident Fellows Program gives researchers an opportunity to engage directly with the organization’s research and policy teams, contribute expertise to emerging technology debates, and strengthen the public-policy impact of their own research.

Applications for the 2026 intake are open until September 18, 2026.

About the Center for Democracy & Technology

The Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) is an organization working at the intersection of technology, public policy, civil liberties, and individual rights.

CDT works to strengthen individual rights and freedoms by defining, promoting, and influencing technology policy and the architecture of the internet that increasingly shapes everyday life. Its areas of focus encompass some of the most significant technology-policy questions facing governments, researchers, companies, civil society organizations, and communities today.

These areas include:

  • Artificial Intelligence Policy and Governance
  • Cybersecurity and Standards
  • Elections and Democracy
  • Equity in Civic Technology
  • Free Expression
  • Government Surveillance
  • Open Internet
  • Privacy and Data

Through its research, advocacy, policy engagement, and collaboration with experts, CDT seeks to ensure that technological development and technology policy protect people’s rights and freedoms.

What Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program?

The CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is a two-year engagement designed to connect leading scholars and academics with CDT’s technology-policy work.

The program provides Fellows with opportunities to bring their research and specialist knowledge directly into CDT’s policy conversations. Fellows can exchange ideas with CDT staff, participate in discussions surrounding emerging issues, and help inform how the organization approaches the social, political, economic, legal, and technical implications of rapidly developing technologies.

CDT intentionally brings together Fellows from diverse academic disciplines, institutions, and areas of expertise.

This interdisciplinary approach reflects the reality that technology policy is no longer confined to computer science or law. Technology influences virtually every aspect of modern society, meaning that understanding its effects requires perspectives from numerous disciplines.

CDT therefore welcomes expertise spanning fields such as:

  • Sociology
  • Psychology
  • Computer science
  • Economics
  • Communications
  • Political science
  • Human-computer interaction
  • Media studies
  • Law
  • Other relevant interdisciplinary fields

Through this diverse community, Fellows can help CDT understand the complex relationship between technology and the institutions, communities, governments, economies, and individuals affected by it.

Bridging Academic Research and Technology Policy

One of the central purposes of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is to help close the gap between academic research and public-interest technology policy.

Academic researchers can produce significant evidence, theories, frameworks, and findings concerning emerging technologies. However, translating that research into policy discussions and practical public-interest outcomes can require connections between scholars and organizations directly involved in policy development.

The Non-Resident Fellows Program creates opportunities for researchers and technology-policy practitioners to learn from each other.

For academics, this can provide greater exposure to policy discussions and the opportunity to understand how research can contribute to practical debates.

For CDT, Fellows provide access to expertise from leading researchers working across a broad range of disciplines.

The program also places Fellows within a wider community of researchers and technology-policy experts, providing opportunities to establish relationships, exchange ideas, and potentially collaborate on some of the most important questions at the intersection of technology and democracy.

Objectives of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

The program is designed for researchers who want to engage directly with and contribute to CDT’s policy work.

CDT Fellows volunteer their time to pursue three broad objectives:

1. Inform and Advance CDT’s Research and Policy Work

Fellows contribute academic knowledge, research findings, disciplinary expertise, and perspectives that can strengthen CDT’s research and policy activities.

Their involvement can help the organization consider technology-policy questions through different academic lenses and incorporate relevant scholarly evidence into its work.

2. Amplify CDT’s Voice and Expand Its Expert Network

Fellows can help connect CDT with leading academics and specialists working on relevant issues.

These relationships can strengthen the exchange of information between academic communities and public-interest technology-policy practitioners.

3. Strengthen the Policy Impact of Fellows’ Research

The relationship is intended to benefit Fellows as well.

CDT aims to work with Fellows to strengthen the public engagement and policy impact of their academic research, potentially helping important scholarly work reach audiences involved in technology-policy conversations.

Who Is CDT Looking For?

CDT is seeking researchers from diverse experiences and backgrounds who are advocating for global digital rights.

Applicants may come from a wide variety of disciplines. Relevant backgrounds include, but are not limited to:

  • Sociology
  • Psychology
  • Computer science
  • Economics
  • Communication
  • Political science
  • Human-computer interaction
  • Media studies
  • Law

The breadth of disciplines reflects CDT’s recognition that digital rights and technology policy involve technical, legal, political, social, economic, cultural, and behavioral considerations.

Minimum Qualifications for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility conditions because this opportunity is specifically targeted at established academics rather than students or early-stage postdoctoral researchers.

Qualified applicants must be prepared to commit to a two-year non-resident engagement with CDT.

Applicants must also:

  • Hold a full-time position at an academic institution.
  • Have published impactful work in peer-reviewed academic venues.
  • Have experience working on technology-policy issues relevant to CDT’s areas of work.
  • Ideally possess a terminal degree, such as a Ph.D., J.D., or equivalent experience within their respective field.
  • Have relevant expertise that can contribute meaningfully to CDT’s research and policy activities.
  • Be able to commit to the requirements of the two-year program.

CDT places particular emphasis on candidates whose technology-policy experience relates to developments in the United States and European Union.

Importantly, the program is not open to current students or postdoctoral researchers.

What Will CDT Non-Resident Fellows Do?

Non-Resident Fellows are expected to become active intellectual contributors to CDT’s broader research and policy community.

Their engagement can include participating in policy strategy calls and joining briefings concerning emerging technology-policy issues.

Fellows are also encouraged to:

  • Contribute original writing to the CDT blog.
  • Present their research and expertise.
  • Participate in collaborative projects with CDT’s research and policy teams.
  • Provide feedback on policy positions.
  • Contribute perspectives on white papers.
  • Provide feedback on research.
  • Review or contribute to other relevant CDT outputs.

These activities provide multiple ways for Fellows to translate academic expertise into practical policy engagement.

Required Contribution During the Two-Year Fellowship

In addition to committing to serve as a Non-Resident Fellow for at least two years, each Fellow agrees to complete at least one specified contribution during the two-year period.

The contribution should concern issues relevant to CDT’s work and be timely.

A Fellow can satisfy this requirement by undertaking at least one of the following:

  1. Co-authoring a CDT blog post or participating in a CDT Tech Talk podcast;
  2. Speaking, presenting, or otherwise contributing to a CDT-branded event; or
  3. Collaborating with CDT on the development of a funding proposal.

These requirements provide Fellows with flexibility to contribute in a way that aligns with their expertise and professional interests.

Participation in CDT Events and Policy Discussions

Fellows may also be invited to participate in CDT-branded events when appropriate.

Examples can include:

  • CDT Working Groups
  • Policy roundtables
  • Public events
  • Webinars
  • Other relevant CDT programs and discussions

Fellows are additionally encouraged to promote CDT through their external professional and academic networks.

This can involve sharing relevant CDT outputs, promoting job, internship, and externship opportunities, and connecting CDT with emerging research, policy conversations, events, or experts within Fellows’ academic institutions and professional networks.

Opportunities for Collaborative Research

The fellowship can extend beyond discussions and events into collaborative research.

CDT Non-Resident Fellows may be invited to conduct research alongside CDT on mutually agreed projects connected to the organization’s core research and advocacy priorities.

Fellows may also proactively propose joint research projects they believe would complement CDT’s work.

However, applicants should understand that proposing a project does not necessarily mean it will automatically proceed. CDT evaluates proposed collaborations in the context of its:

  • Organizational objectives
  • Current priorities
  • Available capacity
  • Resources

This provides room for innovative collaboration while ensuring projects remain aligned with CDT’s broader mission and capabilities.

Memorandum of Understanding for Selected Fellows

Every Non-Resident Fellow will receive a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) at the beginning of their term.

The MOU will establish important aspects of the two-year relationship between the Fellow and CDT.

It will outline:

  • Key dates during the fellowship;
  • Expected deliverables for the two-year term; and
  • Guidelines governing the appropriate use of CDT branding.

This provides Fellows and CDT with a shared framework for expectations and engagement throughout the program.

How CDT Supports Its Non-Resident Fellows

The relationship between CDT and its Fellows is designed to involve active support and engagement rather than simply providing Fellows with a title.

At the beginning of the program, CDT conducts an orientation program.

The orientation includes information concerning:

  • How Non-Resident Fellows work with CDT;
  • How CDT promotes Fellows’ research; and
  • How Fellows can participate in the technology-policy process.

Following orientation, CDT commits to keeping Fellows connected with relevant developments and opportunities.

Access to Technology and Internet Policy Insights

CDT plans to provide Fellows with regular updates regarding important technology and internet-policy developments.

Fellows may also be engaged in relevant working groups and can receive expert insights connected to their research interests.

This exposure can be particularly valuable to academics seeking stronger connections between their research and ongoing policy discussions.

Invitations to CDT Events and Programs

Fellows become active members of CDT’s wider community and can receive invitations to relevant events and programs throughout their participation.

All Fellows are invited as CDT guests to certain public events and webinars, including the organization’s Annual Dinner, Tech Prom.

Fellows will also have opportunities to interact directly with CDT experts.

At the same time, CDT welcomes Fellows’ feedback and recommendations, allowing academics to contribute their perspectives to the organization’s work on developing trends and emerging technology-policy issues.

Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program Remote?

Yes. The opportunity is listed in Washington, District of Columbia, United States, but the position allows remote participation.

This is consistent with the structure of the opportunity as a “Non-Resident” Fellows Program.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully assess whether their professional position, expertise, and availability allow them to participate meaningfully in CDT’s activities throughout the two-year engagement.

Duration of the Program

Selected applicants must commit to serving as CDT Non-Resident Fellows for at least two years.

The two-year structure allows Fellows to establish meaningful relationships with CDT researchers and policy professionals rather than participating through a short-term engagement.

The MOU provided at the beginning of the fellowship will establish the key dates and deliverables applicable to each Fellow’s term.

Application Requirements

Applicants must prepare several important documents.

The required application materials are:

1. Full Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide a comprehensive CV demonstrating their academic background, professional appointments, publications, research experience, relevant policy engagement, and other qualifications.

2. Relevant Writing Sample

Candidates must submit a writing sample relevant to the opportunity.

Given CDT’s emphasis on impactful academic work and technology-policy expertise, applicants should consider selecting a sample that effectively demonstrates their research capabilities and relevant subject-matter knowledge.

3. Cover Letter

Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining:

  • Their interest in becoming a CDT Non-Resident Fellow;
  • Their relevant experience;
  • Their qualifications for the opportunity; and
  • Why their expertise is appropriate for the program.

Applicants should ensure that their cover letter clearly communicates how their academic expertise intersects with technology policy and CDT’s areas of work.

Important Document Submission Requirement

There is an important formatting requirement applicants should not overlook.

The CV, writing sample, and cover letter must be compiled into one PDF or document for submission.

Applicants should therefore not prepare these documents as unrelated individual uploads unless the application system specifically instructs otherwise.

Combining everything into a single organized file before beginning the final submission process can help ensure compliance with CDT’s stated application instructions.

How to Apply for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026

Interested researchers should complete the application through CDT’s official recruitment system.

A practical application process would involve:

  1. Review the fellowship requirements carefully.
  2. Confirm that you hold a full-time academic position.
  3. Assess whether your research experience relates meaningfully to CDT’s technology-policy priorities.
  4. Update your full academic CV.
  5. Select a relevant and strong writing sample.
  6. Prepare a tailored cover letter explaining your interest, expertise, and qualifications.
  7. Compile the CV, writing sample, and cover letter into one PDF or document.
  8. Access the official CDT careers page and locate the Non-Resident Fellows Program opening.
  9. Select “Apply for this position.”
  10. Complete the required application information and submit the combined document before the deadline.

Applicants with questions about the program or application process can contact CDT’s research team at research@cdt.org.

APPLY NOW

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Center for Democracy & Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is Friday, September 18, 2026.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to prepare their materials well before the closing date, particularly because the application requires a CV, relevant writing sample, and tailored cover letter compiled into one document.

Why Researchers Should Consider the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

For academics whose work intersects with digital rights and technology policy, the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program provides an opportunity to move beyond traditional academic publication and participate in broader policy conversations.

Several aspects distinguish the program.

Direct Engagement With Technology Policy

Fellows can participate in strategy calls, emerging-issue briefings, policy discussions, and other activities that bring academic expertise closer to practical technology-policy work.

Greater Policy Impact for Academic Research

Researchers often seek ways to ensure their scholarship reaches audiences beyond academic journals and conferences.

Through CDT, Fellows can explore opportunities to strengthen the public engagement and policy relevance of their work.

Interdisciplinary Collaboration

Technology policy requires perspectives from numerous fields.

Researchers can become part of a community spanning law, political science, sociology, economics, psychology, communications, computer science, human-computer interaction, media studies, and other disciplines.

Opportunities to Publish and Present

Fellows may contribute to CDT’s blog, participate in Tech Talk, present at CDT events, and engage in other public-facing opportunities.

Potential Research Collaboration

Researchers may have opportunities to collaborate with CDT on mutually agreed research projects and can propose projects relevant to the organization’s priorities.

Access to a Wider Technology-Policy Community

Participation connects Fellows with CDT experts and a broader network of researchers and technology-policy professionals.

Diversity, Equity and Inclusion

CDT states that it is an equal opportunity and inclusive employer and does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, gender, gender expression, age, national origin, disability, marital status, or sexual orientation.

The organization specifically states that it believes diversity enables stronger and more impactful work.

Women, people of color, disabled people, members of low-income communities, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and members of other marginalized communities are strongly encouraged to apply.

Key Details at a Glance

Program: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026

Organization: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT)

Listed Location: Washington, District of Columbia, United States

Participation: Remote participation allowed

Duration: At least two years

Target Group: Established academics and researchers holding full-time positions at academic institutions

Primary Focus: Technology policy, digital rights, academic research, and public-interest technology policy

Required Documents: Full CV, relevant writing sample, and cover letter

Submission Format: Required materials must be compiled into one PDF or document

Application Deadline: September 18, 2026

Conclusion

The Center for Democracy & Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 provides established academics and researchers with an opportunity to connect rigorous scholarly research with real-world technology-policy discussions.

As questions surrounding artificial intelligence, privacy, cybersecurity, online expression, surveillance, democracy, data governance, digital equity, and the open internet become increasingly important, interdisciplinary academic expertise has an important role to play in shaping informed public policy.

Through its two-year Non-Resident Fellows Program, CDT aims to bring researchers directly into this environment. Selected Fellows can engage with CDT experts, participate in policy strategy discussions and emerging-issue briefings, contribute original writing and presentations, collaborate on relevant initiatives, and help strengthen the connection between academic evidence and public-interest technology policy.

At the same time, Fellows can benefit from closer exposure to policy conversations, opportunities to strengthen the reach and impact of their own research, and relationships with a broader community of academics and technology-policy professionals.

Researchers with impactful peer-reviewed work, relevant technology-policy experience, and a full-time position at an academic institution should consider preparing their application materials early.

Applications must include a full CV, relevant writing sample, and cover letter compiled into one document, and must be submitted by September 18, 2026.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.
